reference.source: Occupational and Environmental Respiratory Medicine reference texts
clinicalPearls: Occurs in workers exposed to hard metal, an alloy of tungsten carbide bound with cobalt, used in cutting tools, drill bits, and diamond polishing
Cobalt is regarded as the key sensitising and toxic component driving lung injury
Presents as an interstitial lung disease with cough and progressive exertional breathlessness, sometimes with an occupational asthma phenotype
The histological hallmark is giant-cell interstitial pneumonia, with bizarre multinucleated giant cells and cannibalistic cell-in-cell appearances
Bronchoalveolar lavage may reveal characteristic multinucleated giant cells and support the diagnosis
Disease can occur even with low measured exposure, and susceptibility appears to have an immunological or individual component
Diamond polishers using cobalt-containing discs can develop similar disease even without tungsten carbide (cobalt lung)
reference.pathophysiology: Inhaled cobalt, particularly in combination with tungsten carbide, generates reactive oxygen species and acts as a haptenic sensitiser, provoking both toxic and immune-mediated injury to alveolar and bronchiolar epithelium. The resulting inflammatory response produces interstitial fibrosis and the distinctive giant-cell interstitial pneumonia pattern, characterised by numerous multinucleated giant cells within alveolar spaces and interstitium, some engulfing other inflammatory cells. Continued exposure drives progressive fibrosis, while an asthmatic or hypersensitivity component reflects the sensitising nature of cobalt. Individual susceptibility means severity does not correlate simply with measured dust levels.
additionalDifferentials: Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT to define the interstitial pattern and fibrosis
Bronchoalveolar lavage looking for multinucleated giant cells
Lung biopsy demonstrating giant-cell interstitial pneumonia when needed
Detailed occupational history and workplace exposure assessment
Pulmonary function tests including diffusing capacity
Cobalt exposure biomarkers (urine or blood cobalt) where available
redFlags: Rapidly progressive breathlessness and hypoxaemia indicating accelerating fibrosis
Continued workplace exposure despite established disease
Development of respiratory failure or cor pulmonale
Features suggesting superimposed infection in an immunosuppressed treated patient
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies from stabilisation or improvement after exposure cessation and corticosteroids to relentless progression to fibrosis and respiratory failure; early recognition and removal from exposure offer the best chance of recovery.
pitfalls: Missing the occupational link and labelling the disease idiopathic interstitial pneumonia
Assuming low measured cobalt levels exclude the diagnosis
Overlooking a coexisting occupational asthma component
Allowing continued exposure, which perpetuates injury despite treatment
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Remove the worker from cobalt and hard metal exposure, as cessation of exposure is the single most important intervention
Give systemic corticosteroids to suppress the active giant-cell interstitial pneumonia and inflammatory component
Provide supportive care with supplemental oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation, and inhaled therapy for any airflow-obstruction or occupational-asthma phenotype
Monitor with serial pulmonary function including diffusing capacity and high-resolution CT to track fibrosis
Undertake workplace exposure control and report as an occupational lung disease
Manage jointly through a multidisciplinary team of respiratory and occupational medicine specialists
Refer for antifibrotic consideration or lung transplantation assessment when fibrosis progresses towards respiratory failure
